--- title: "Use Ragnar To Build Chatbots For Your Quarto Book" subtitle: "Grounding an AI assistant in your documentation" author: "Martin Frigaard" date: "2026-08-07" categories: ["Shiny", "ragnar", "RAG", "AI", "LLM"] toc: true image: "image.png" toc-depth: 4 toc-expand: true callout-icon: false code-block-bg: "#f8f8f8" code-block-border-left: "#e8e8e8" draft: false freeze: true knitr: opts_chunk: fig-dpi: 320 fig-width: 6 out-width: '85%' fig-format: png fig-align: 'center' --- If you've published technical documentation with Quarto (like my [Shiny App-Packages book](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/)) you've probably wished readers could ask it questions directly. A chatbot would be ideal; unfortunately, LLMs trained on public data might hallucinate when asked specific questions in reference to your documentation.[^1] [^1]: i.e., they might confidently describe a pattern from the documentation incorrectly, or even invent function arguments that don't exist. [Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation) solves this problem. Instead of relying on training data, RAG feeds *your* actual documentation into the LLM before generating a response. The result is a chatbot that answers accurately, cites the exact section it pulled from, and updates instantly as your book evolves. In this post I'll cover how to build a chatbot using [`{ragnar}`](https://ragnar.tidyverse.org/), an R package that handles the entire RAG pipeline. I'll show two deployment paths: one using a model API key (from Anthropic/Claude or OpenAI/GPT), and one using local models via [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) for privacy and cost control. We'll use the [`quartohelp` project](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/quartohelp) as our reference implementation. ## What is RAG RAG is a three-step process: 1) retrieve relevant excerpts from the documentation, 2) feed those excerpts to an LLM, and 3) let the LLM synthesize a response grounded in the *actual* content. ### Why this matters Without RAG, an LLM responds based on what it learned during training. For specialized topics like building Shiny apps as R packages[^sap], this creates a reliability problem. The LLM might confidently describe module patterns from the book incorrectly because the training data was incomplete or conflicting. [^sap]: In truth, this topic isn't so specialized that an LLM couldn't give best practices. [Mastering Shiny](https://mastering-shiny.org/) and [R Packages, 2e](https://r-pkgs.org/index.html) have almost certainly been included in the training data. And if they haven't, the [Shiny source code](https://github.com/rstudio/shiny) and [Writing R Extensions](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-devel/R-exts.html) definitely have. ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'Traditional LLM' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%% graph LR subgraph traditional ["Traditional LLM"] Q1(["User
Query"]) -->|relies on| T[("Training Data")] T --> A(["LLM Response
(hallucination
risk)"]) A -->|answer| Q1 end style traditional fill:#fff style Q1 fill:#dfdfde style T fill:#b3cde0 style A fill:#ffcccc ``` With RAG, the LLM sees the *actual* text before responding. If we ask *"where do I put external resources in my Shiny app/R package?"*, the retrieval step finds the exact section of the book that covers this, passes this to the LLM, and the LLM synthesizes an answer directly from that content. If/when the documentation updates, the chatbot reflects those changes immediately without retraining. ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'RAG' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%% graph LR subgraph rag ["RAG Pipeline"] Q2(["User
Query"]) B[\"Your Documentation"\] C(["LLM Response
(grounded &
accurate)"]) Q2 -->|"Retrieve relevant
excerpts"| B B -->|feeds| C C -->|answer| Q2 end style rag fill:#fff style Q2 fill:#dfdfde style C fill:#ccffcc ``` The trade-off is complexity. RAG requires three additional components: a document chunking strategy, an embedding model to convert text to vectors, and a retrieval system to find relevant chunks. `{ragnar}` abstracts away most of this, but you'll need to understand the basic concepts. ## The `{ragnar}` workflow `{ragnar}` implements RAG in seven sequential steps. Understanding this pipeline helped me configure it for my documentation.[^ragnar-process] [^ragnar-process]: Read more in [Why RAG? The Hallucination Problem](https://ragnar.tidyverse.org/articles/ragnar.html#why-rag-the-hallucination-problem). Here's what each step does: 1. **Document input**: `{ragnar}` accepts Quarto or Markdown files as input. For my [Shiny App-Packages book](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/shiny-app-pkgs), this means pointing `{ragnar}` at the `.qmd` files. 2. **Markdown conversion**: Files are converted to a consistent Markdown format, preserving structure and headings. 3. **Text chunking**: Long documents are split into smaller chunks. `{ragnar}` uses semantic chunking (breaking at logical section boundaries) rather than naive word-count splitting. This is important, because if the documentation has small subsections, those become natural chunk boundaries. Well-defined chunk boundaries are what makes the retrieval more precise. ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'ragnar Workflow' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '14px'}}}%% graph TD A(["Document Input
.qmd files"]) --> B("Markdown Conversion") B --> C("Text Chunking
semantic boundaries") style A fill:#b2e7cd style B fill:#fff style C fill:#fbd6c2 ``` 4. **Context augmentation**: Each chunk is tagged with its heading hierarchy, which preserves context. For example, when the retrieval step finds a chunk about documenting Shiny app functions, it knows it came from the "Documenting app functions" section of [Chapter 5.](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/document.html#sec-document-app-functions) 5. **Embedding**: Chunks are converted to high-dimensional vector representations. This is where the embedding model (Claude, GPT, or local) enters the pipeline. Vectors capture meaning, and similar chunks have similar vectors, even if they use different words. 6. **Storage**: Vectors and chunks are stored in a `{duckdb}` database. This is the retrieval index; it lives on disk and can be updated incrementally as the documentation evolves. ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'ragnar Workflow' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '14px'}}}%% graph TD C("Text Chunking
semantic boundaries") D("Context Augmentation
heading hierarchy") C --> D D --> E["Embeddings Vectors
Claude or Ollama"] E --> F[("DuckDB Storage
local index")] style C fill:#b2e7cd style D fill:#fff style E fill:#fff style F fill:#fbd6c2 ``` 7. **Retrieval and chat**: At runtime, user queries are embedded using the same model, then compared to stored vectors using cosine similarity (vector math for "*how similar are these concepts*"). `{ragnar}` also performs keyword matching as a fallback. Top results are passed to the LLM along with the user query. ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'ragnar Workflow' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '14px'}}}%% graph TD F[("DuckDB Storage
local index")] F --> G("Retrieval
semantic + keyword
cosine similarity") G --> H(["LLM Chat
synthesis grounded
response"]) style F fill:#b2e7cd style G fill:#fff style H fill:#fbd6c2 ``` Notice that the embeddings and retrieval happen *before* generation. The LLM never touches the raw documentation; it only sees the relevant excerpts that the retriever found. ## Setting up `{ragnar}` with API Keys LLM Model providers (Claude from Anthropic or GPT from OpenAI) give the highest quality responses and the easiest setup. We just need an API key, but `{ragnar}` handles the rest. ### Prerequisites Install `{ragnar}` and required dependencies: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} install.packages(c("ragnar", "duckdb")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} library(ragnar) library(duckdb) ``` ::: We'll also need either an Anthropic API key (for Claude) or OpenAI key (for GPT). Set the API key as an environment variable before starting: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="your-key-here" ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-key-here" ``` ::: ### Building a retrieval index The first time we set up `{ragnar}`, we'll ingest the book's `.qmd` files and build a retrieval index. This is a one-time setup step. After this, we only need to rebuild if the book content changes. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} :::: {.callout-important collapse='false' appearance='default' icon=false} ## [Requirement]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.10em; color: #282b2d;'} `{ragnar}` requires `{duckdb}` for storage; RSQLite and PostgreSQL are not supported alternatives. `{duckdb}` is chosen specifically for its vector similarity search capabilities, which power the retrieval step. If you need cloud storage instead of a local file, `{ragnar}` supports MotherDuck (cloud-hosted `{duckdb}`). ::: :::: ::: The code below ingests the `shiny-app-packages` book and builds an embedded index. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # build embedded index ----- book_path <- "~/path/to/shiny-app-pkgs" #<1> chunks <- markdown_chunk( #<2> dir = book_path, pattern = "\\.qmd$" ) #<2> embedded <- embed_anthropic( #<3> chunks, model = "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022" ) #<3> store <- ragnar_store_create( #<4> embedded, path = "shiny-book-index.duckdb" ) #<4> ``` ::: 1. Point to the book's `.qmd` files\ 2. Finds all `.qmd` files in the book directory; converts them to chunks with heading context preserved.\ 3. Sends chunks to Anthropic API for embedding (this costs a few cents for a typical book), gets back vectors.\ 4. Creates a local `{duckdb}` file that serves as the retrieval index. The store is now ready. We can query it without additional API calls; only live chat with Claude requires the API. ### Running the chatbot Once the index is built, we can launch an interactive chat session: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # run the chatbot -------------- store <- ragnar_store_open("shiny-book-index.duckdb") #<1> chat <- ragnar_chat_create( #<2> store = store, model = "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022", provider = "anthropic" ) #<2> response <- ragnar_chat_message( #<3> chat, "How do I structure file names for R6 class modules in a Shiny app-package?" ) #<3> ``` ::: 1. Load our stored index\ 2. Start a chat session (creates a chat session bound to our index and Claude model)\ 3. Ask a question. The query is embedded and compared to stored vectors; top matches feed into Claude along with the query. The contents of `response` include: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} response$answer #<1> response$sources #<2> response$citations #<3> ``` ::: 1. `$answer`: Claude's response grounded in your book\ 2. `$sources`: List of chunks used to generate the response\ 3. `$citations`: Links back to the `.qmd` files Claude generates a response grounded in our actual documentation, not training data. ## Setting up `{ragnar}` locally For privacy-conscious deployments or when API costs matter, we can run embeddings and chat locally using Ollama. **This approach keeps the data on our machine and has no per-query costs.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} :::: {.callout-note collapse='false' appearance='default' icon=false} ## [Trade-offs]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.10em; color: #282b2d;'} Local models are slower (seconds instead of milliseconds) and usually less capable at synthesis than API model keys. Response quality is good but not exceptional. Use this when privacy or cost is the priority. ::: :::: ::: ### Installing Ollama Download and install Ollama from . Then pull a model: Pull the [`nomic-embed-text` model](https://ollama.com/library/nomic-embed-text) (it's a capable open model for embeddings): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} ollama pull nomic-embed-text ``` ::: Pull a chat model (e.g., [`mistral`](https://ollama.com/library/mistral) or [`neural-chat`](https://ollama.com/library/neural-chat)) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} ollama pull mistral ``` ::: Start the Ollama server: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} ollama serve ``` ::: Ollama listens on `localhost:11434` by default. ### Building the index locally The setup is similar to the API key approach, but `{ragnar}` calls a local Ollama instance instead of Anthropic: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Build the local index ---------------- chunks <- markdown_chunk( #<1> dir = "~/path/to/shiny-app-pkgs", pattern = "\\.qmd$" ) #<1> embedded <- embed_ollama( #<2> chunks, base_url = "http://localhost:11434", #<3> model = "nomic-embed-text" ) #<2> store <- ragnar_store_create( #<4> embedded, path = "shiny-book-local.duckdb" ) #<4> ``` ::: 1. Chunk the book 2. Embed locally via Ollama 3. Ollama server URL; ensure `ollama serve` is running before this step 4. Store in `{duckdb}` (same as before) This step is slower than cloud embeddings (several minutes for a typical book) but runs entirely on the local machine. ### Running local chat Once the index is built, chat is just as simple: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Run chat locally ----------- store <- ragnar_store_open("shiny-book-local.duckdb") #<1> chat <- ragnar_chat_create( #<2> store = store, model = "mistral", #<3> provider = "ollama", base_url = "http://localhost:11434" ) #<2> response <- ragnar_chat_message( #<4> chat, "Explain the difference between module-based and R6-based architecture in Shiny app-packages." ) #<4> ``` ::: 1. Load locally stored index 2. Build `chat` from local `store` and specify `model` 3. You can swap `mistral` for another Ollama model (e.g., `neural-chat`, `llama2`) 4. Ask a question and store the `response` We can view the `answer` in the `response`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} response$answer ``` ::: The workflow is identical; only the model and provider change. No API keys, no cloud calls, and the documentation content never leaves our machine. ## API Keys vs. Local models Here's a practical comparison: | Dimension | API Key (Claude/GPT) | Local (Ollama) | |--------------------|---------------------------------|----------------------| | Setup | API key + one command | Download + server | | Speed | \~1 sec per query | \~5-10 sec per query | | Quality | Excellent | Good | | Cost | \~\$0.01-0.05 per 1K embeddings | Free after setup | | Privacy | Data sent to provider | All local | | Hallucination risk | Low | Moderate | | Maintenance | None (provider manages) | Keep Ollama updated |
:::{layout="[50,50]" layout-valign="top"} ### Use API model keys when - Response quality matters most; i.e., publishing the chatbot publicly - Speed is important; users expect sub-second responses - Cost is not a concern (typical book: \$0.50 setup + \$0.001 per chat turn) - Cloud API calls aren't a concern ### Use local models when - Privacy is mandatory; data cannot leave the network - Testing or building an internal tool - Cost is a concern (local models have zero per-query costs) - The available server can run Ollama (CPU is fine, GPU is better) ::: For the `shiny-app-packages` book, I started with Claude. The setup was simple, quality was excellent, and costs are negligible for a published resource. Later, if I want to offer an offline or private version, Ollama provides a clear fallback. ### Deployment architectures The two approaches differ in where computation happens and how data flows. Model keys send queries and receive responses from cloud APIs, but the index stays local. ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'Model API' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '13px'}}}%% graph LR subgraph cloud ["Model API (Claude/GPT)"] direction TB U1(["Your Machine"]) B1[("duckdb Index
with embeddings
stored locally")] U1 -->|"i. query"| B1 B1 -->|"ii. retrieve chunks
similarity search"| U1 U1 -->|"iii. query + chunks"| C1{{"Anthropic/OpenAI
Servers"}} C1 -->|"iv. response"| U1 end style cloud fill:#fff style C1 fill:#fff0e8 style B1 fill:#b3cde0 ``` Local models keep everything on our machine; Ollama never touches the internet: ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'Local Models' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '13px'}}}%% graph LR subgraph local ["Local Models (Ollama)"] direction TB U2(["Your Machine"]) B2[("duckdb Index
with embeddings
stored locally")] U2 -->|"i. query"| B2 B2 -->|"ii. retrieve chunks
similarity search"| U2 U2 -->|"iii. query + chunks"| O{{"Ollama Server
localhost:11434"}} O -->|"iv. response"| U2 end style local fill:#fff style O fill:#f0f8e8 style B2 fill:#b3cde0 ``` ## Integrating with book site The [`quartohelp` project](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/quartohelp) shows one complete working example: it builds the index during the site build, serves it through a Quarto extension, and embeds a chat widget directly in the rendered pages. ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'quartohelp approach: integrated site build and chat' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%% graph TD author(["Author
Writes documentation"]) -->|"quarto render"| build("Site
build process") build -->|"Build index"| chunk("Chunk and embed
during render") chunk -->|"Create"| index[("Index
in memory")] index -->|"Register"| ext("Quarto Extension") ext -->|"Inject"| pages("Rendered HTML pages
with chat widget") pages -->|"Read + query"| reader(["Reader
Uses chat widget
on the page"]) style author fill:#dfdfde style build fill:#fff style chunk fill:#fff style index fill:#b3cde0 style ext fill:#fbd6c2 style pages fill:#ccffcc style reader fill:#dfdfde ``` This is an elegant approach, but it couples the chatbot to the site build, which means every render is also an embedding job and every change to the widget is a change to the book. I reached for a simpler approach: Publish the index as a static file alongside the site, then let a separately deployed Shiny app read that file and do the querying. This way, the book stays a book, and the chatbot stays an app. Division of labor. ### Why a decoupled index works The `{duckdb}` index is a single file. Once the embeddings are computed, these files are immutable until the documentation changes, so nothing about it needs a server. GitHub Pages (or Netlify, or S3) already serves static files well, and publishing the index costs nothing beyond the storage. Splitting the process into two pieces has three advantages: 1. **Decoupling**: Rendering the book never triggers an embedding run, so `quarto render` stays fast and stays free of API keys. Breaking the chat app never breaks the book. 2. **Simplicity**: There's no Quarto extension to maintain, no JavaScript bridge between the page and the index, and no per-reader retrieval running in the browser. The Shiny app is an ordinary Shiny app. 3. **Maintenance**: The index and the app version independently. We can redeploy the app with a new model or a nicer UI without rebuilding embeddings, and we can rebuild embeddings without redeploying the app. ```{mermaid} %%| eval: true %%| fig-align: 'center' %%| fig-caption: 'Build-time workflow: author to published index' %%| echo: false %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%% graph TD author(["Author
Local Machine"]) -->|"i. Build Index"| chunk("Chunk documentation
Embed via Claude/Ollama") chunk -->|"ii. Create file"| duckdb[("shiny-book-index.duckdb")] duckdb -->|"iii. Commit to repo"| repo("Git
Repository") repo -->|"iv. Site build"| build("Quarto/Hugo
build process") build -->|"v. Publish"| publish[("Published Index
https://site.com/assets/index.duckdb")] style author fill:#dfdfde style chunk fill:#fff style duckdb fill:#b3cde0 style repo fill:#fff style build fill:#fff style publish fill:#fbd6c2 ``` The **Published Index** is a hyperlink: `https://site.com/assets/index.duckdb` The trade-off? Readers leave the book to use the chatbot, or interact with it through an embedded iframe rather than a native widget. For most documentation sites, that's a fair price. ### Publishing the index with the site To build the index locally as mentioned above, we can write it into a directory that Quarto will publish. I put mine under `assets/` at the book root. ```bash shiny-app-pkgs/ ├── _quarto.yml ├── index.qmd ├── document.qmd ├── assets/ │ ├── shiny-book-index.duckdb │ └── index-version.txt └── ... ``` Quarto copies all the files it doesn't render, but being explicit avoids surprises. So we add the directory to the `resources` key in `_quarto.yml`: ```yaml project: type: book resources: - assets/shiny-book-index.duckdb - assets/index-version.txt ``` The `index-version.txt` file holds a timestamp or commit SHA written at build time. The app uses it to decide whether its cached copy is stale. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # rebuild index ---- chunks <- markdown_chunk(dir = ".", pattern = "\\.qmd$") embedded <- embed_anthropic(chunks, model = "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022") store <- ragnar_store_create(embedded, path = "assets/shiny-book-index.duckdb") writeLines(format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d%H%M%S"), "assets/index-version.txt") ``` ::: Commit both files, push, and publish the site. The index is now a URL: ```{.default} https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/assets/shiny-book-index.duckdb ``` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='default' icon=false} ## [Watch the file size]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.10em; color: #282b2d;'} Embeddings are dense; a book-sized index can run tens of megabytes, and GitHub warns above 50 MB and rejects files above 100 MB. If the index outgrows the repo, store it with [Git LFS](https://git-lfs.com/) or attach it to a GitHub Release and point the app at the release asset URL instead. The rest of the workflow is unchanged. ::: :::: ::: ### Querying the index from Shiny With the Shiny method, the app downloads the published file once at startup, opens it read only, and passes the store to a module. We can put the download in `global.R` (or `app.R` above `ui`), so it runs once per process rather than once per user session. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # global.R ---- library(shiny) library(ragnar) base_url <- "https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/assets" index_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "shiny-book-index.duckdb") #<1> remote_version <- readLines(file.path(base_url, "index-version.txt"))[1] #<2> cached_version <- file.path(tempdir(), "index-version.txt") stale <- !file.exists(index_path) || !identical(remote_version, readLines(cached_version)[1]) #<3> if (stale) { curl::curl_download(file.path(base_url, "shiny-book-index.duckdb"), index_path) writeLines(remote_version, cached_version) } store <- ragnar_store_open(index_path, read_only = TRUE) #<4> ``` ::: 1. `{duckdb}` needs a file on disk, so the app writes to its own temp directory\ 2. One small HTTP request tells us whether the published index has moved\ 3. Download only when the cached copy is missing or out of date\ 4. Opening read only means every user session can share this connection safely The data flow is short because we're building locally, committing, publishing the data with the site, downloading once at app startup, and querying in memory from then on. Readers never touch the book repo, and the app never writes back to the index. The module handles the query itself. Each user gets their own chat session so conversation history doesn't leak between readers, but they all read from the same `store`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="show/hide chat module"} # R/mod_ragnar_chat.R ---- mod_ragnar_chat_ui <- function(id) { ns <- NS(id) tagList( textAreaInput(ns("query"), "Ask the book a question", width = "100%", rows = 3), actionButton(ns("ask"), "Ask", class = "btn-primary"), uiOutput(ns("answer")), uiOutput(ns("sources")) ) } mod_ragnar_chat_server <- function(id, store) { moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) { chat <- ragnar_chat_create( #<1> store = store, model = "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022", provider = "anthropic" ) #<1> response <- eventReactive(input$ask, { #<2> req(nzchar(input$query)) ragnar_chat_message(chat, input$query) }) #<2> output$answer <- renderUI({ markdown(response()$answer) }) output$sources <- renderUI({ #<3> tags$ul( lapply(response()$citations, \(cite) tags$li(tags$a(href = cite, cite))) ) }) #<3> }) } ``` ::: 1. Created inside `moduleServer()`, so the session is per user\ 2. `eventReactive()` keeps the app from calling the API on every keystroke\ 3. Citations are the payoff of RAG; always show the reader where the answer came from We can wire it up in an unremarkable app interface: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} ui <- fluidPage( titlePanel("Ask Shiny App-Packages"), mod_ragnar_chat_ui("chat") ) server <- function(input, output, session) { mod_ragnar_chat_server("chat", store = store) } shinyApp(ui, server) ``` ::: For deployment, use the [`{rsconnect}`](https://rstudio.github.io/rsconnect/) package to deploy to Posit Connect or Connect Cloud. Run the following: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} rsconnect::deployApp() ``` ::: Before deploying, set an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable in the deployment platform's secrets manager (not in the code). On Connect Cloud, this goes in the app's Environment Variables settings on the dashboard. Link to the deployed app from the book's navbar (or embed it in a page with an `
